claim: 92 annotated 3D images at cellular resolution were generated in Arabidopsis to study ovule primordium development.
source: We generated 92 annotated 3D images at cellular resolution in Arabidopsis.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number and type of images generated as part of the study methodology.

claim: A spatio-temporal pattern of cell division acts in a domain-specific manner as the ovule primordium forms.
source: We identified the spatio-temporal pattern of cell division that acts in a domain-specific manner as the primordium forms.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental observations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Tissue growth models uncovered plausible morphogenetic principles involving a spatially confined growth signal, differential mechanical properties, and cell growth anisotropy.
source: Tissue growth models uncovered plausible morphogenetic principles involving a spatially confined growth signal, differential mechanical properties, and cell growth anisotropy.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: SMC characteristics first arise in more than one cell during ovule primordium development.
source: Our analysis revealed that SMC characteristics first arise in more than one cell but SMC fate becomes progressively restricted to a single cell during organ growth.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through quantitative analysis in the results section.

claim: SMC fate becomes progressively restricted to a single cell during organ growth.
source: Our analysis revealed that SMC characteristics first arise in more than one cell but SMC fate becomes progressively restricted to a single cell during organ growth.
evidence: This progressive restriction is documented through developmental stage analysis and quantification.

claim: Altered primordium geometry in katanin mutants coincides with a delay in the fate restriction process.
source: Altered primordium geometry coincided with a delay in the fate restriction process in katanin mutants.
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated through comparative analysis of wild-type and katanin mutant primordia.

claim: Tissue geometry channels reproductive cell fate in the Arabidopsis ovule primordium.
source: Altogether, our study suggests that tissue geometry channels reproductive cell fate in the Arabidopsis ovule primordium.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple lines of evidence including modeling and mutant analysis.

claim: In flowering plants, the female germline precursor differentiates as a single spore mother cell (SMC) as the ovule primordium forms.
source: In flowering plants, the female germline precursor differentiates as a single spore mother cell (SMC) as the ovule primordium forms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant reproduction stated in the abstract.

claim: In animals, primordial germ cells (PGCs) are set-aside during embryogenesis from a mass of pluripotent cells.
source: In animals, primordial germ cells (PGCs) are set-aside during embryogenesis from a mass of pluripotent cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about animal development used for comparison.

claim: The SMC is recognizable as a single, large, and elongated subepidermal cell, which is centrally positioned within the nucellus and displays a prominent nucleus and nucleolus.
source: The SMC is recognizable as a single, large, and elongated subepidermal cell, which is centrally positioned within the nucellus and displays a prominent nucleus and nucleolus (Bajon et al., 1999; Bowman, 1993; Schmidt et al., 2015; Schneitz et al., 1995).
evidence: This description is supported by cited literature and confirmed by observations in this study.

claim: More than one SMC candidate per primordium is occasionally seen at different frequencies depending on the specific Arabidopsis accession (~5% in Landsberg erecta [Ler], 10% in Columbia [Col-0], 27% in Monterrosso [Mr-0]).
source: Although SMC singleness may appear to be robust, more than one SMC candidate per primordium is occasionally seen, yet at different frequencies depending on the specific Arabidopsis accession (~5% in Landsberg erecta [Ler], 10% in Columbia [Col-0], 27% in Monterrosso [Mr-0]), (Grossniklaus and Schneitz, 1998; Rodríguez-Leal et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by cited literature documenting accession-specific variation.

claim: Arabidopsis, maize, and rice mutants in which SMC singleness is compromised have unveiled the role of regulatory pathways involving intercellular signaling, small RNAs, as well as DNA and histone methylation.
source: Arabidopsis, maize, and rice mutants in which SMC singleness is compromised have unveiled the role of regulatory pathways involving intercellular signaling, small RNAs, as well as DNA and histone methylation (Garcia-Aguilar et al., 2010; Mendes et al., 2020; Nonomura et al., 2003; Olmedo-Monfil et al., 2010; Schmidt et al., 2011; Sheridan et al., 1996; Sheridan et al., 1999; Su et al., 2020; Su et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from multiple cited studies on SMC regulation.

claim: Cell-cycle regulation contributes to the stabilization of SMC fate in a cell-autonomous manner through cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors and RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED1 (RBR1).
source: As the SMC forms, cell-cycle regulation contributes to the stabilization of its fate in a cell-autonomous manner through cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitors and RETINOBLASTOMA-RELATED1 (RBR1) (Cao et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: This mechanism is supported by cited literature on cell cycle control in SMC.

claim: SMC singleness results from a two-step control: first, by restricting differentiation to one cell and second, by preventing self-renewal before meiosis.
source: SMC singleness thus appears to result from a two-step control: first, by restricting differentiation to one cell and second, by preventing self-renewal before meiosis (reviewed in Lora et al., 2019; Pinto et al., 2019).
evidence: This model is based on review articles synthesizing current understanding.

claim: The current knowledge of ovule primordium growth in Arabidopsis is based on two-dimensional (2D) micrographs from tissue sections or clearing.
source: Our current knowledge of ovule primordium growth in Arabidopsis is based on two-dimensional (2D) micrographs from tissue sections or clearing.
evidence: This describes the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: A 3D analysis of average cell volumes during primordium growth was recently provided.
source: In addition, a 3D analysis of average cell volumes during primordium growth was recently provided (Lora et al., 2017), and extensive 3D analysis was carried on for late ovule stages (Vijayan et al., 2021).
evidence: This acknowledges recent related work in the field.

claim: The reference collection comprises 92 segmented images with a total of 7763 annotated cells and five morphological cell descriptors.
source: The collection of 92 segmented images, comprising a total of 7763 annotated cells and five morphological cell descriptors (volume, area, sphericity, prolate and oblate ellipticity), provides a unique resource for morphodynamic analyses of ovule primordium growth.
evidence: This quantifies the data resource generated by the study.

claim: The SMC appears morphologically distinct at late stages (2-I and 2-II) but not at early stages based on PCA analysis.
source: In this global analysis, the SMC appears morphologically distinct at late stages (2-I and 2-II) but not at early stages.
evidence: This finding is based on principal component analysis of cell descriptors shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Phase I (stages 0-I to 0-III) is characterized by a 4.5-fold increase in total cell number together with a moderate increase in mean cell volume (10%, p=0.03).
source: Phase I (stages 0-I to 0-III) is characterized by a 4.5-fold increase in total cell number together with a moderate increase in mean cell volume (10%, p=0.03).
evidence: This quantitative finding is based on analysis of segmented images with statistical significance.

claim: Phase II (stages 1-I to 2-II) is characterized by a moderate increase in cell number (50%) and the global mean cell volume is relatively constant.
source: By contrast, Phase II (stages 1-I to 2-II) is characterized by a moderate increase in cell number (50%) and the global mean cell volume is relatively constant (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This finding is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Anisotropic organ growth during Phase I is confirmed by a steady increase in height, while primordium width increases moderately.
source: Anisotropic organ growth during Phase I was confirmed by a steady increase in height, while primordium width increased moderately (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements of organ dimensions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Phase I, a high proliferation activity was scored in L1 cells at the primordium apex (scoring 64% of all mitotic events).
source: Consistent with our previous observation, in Phase I, a high proliferation activity was scored in L1 cells at the primordium apex (scoring 64% of all mitotic events).
evidence: This is based on quantification of the CYCB1.1db-GFP mitotic reporter.

claim: The L2 apical domain remains relatively quiescent during Phase I (only 3% of the mitotic events).
source: By contrast, the L2 apical domain remains relatively quiescent (only 3% of the mitotic events).
evidence: This is based on mitotic activity mapping using the CYCB1.1db-GFP reporter.

claim: During Phase II, the majority (60%) of mitotic events is found in the basal domain.
source: During Phase II, the majority (60%) of mitotic events is found in the basal domain, consistent with the progressive population of the basal domain with more cells.
evidence: This finding is based on mitotic activity quantification shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The distinct size of the SMC candidate is already detected at stage 0-III when compared to other L2,L3 cells.
source: The distinct size of the SMC candidate is already detected at stage 0-III when compared to other L2,L3 cells (Figure 2I), or even earlier (stage 0-I) when compared to all other cells (Figure 2I inset).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell volume measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Cells from the L2 and L3 layers are larger than L1 cells already at stage 0-I.
source: In addition, cells from the L2 and L3 layers are larger than L1 cells already at stage 0-I (Figure 2J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), possibly due to a longer growth phase, consistent with the low division frequency observed previously.
evidence: This is based on cell volume comparisons shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The SMC has a consistent anisotropic shape from early stages onwards, with a distinguishable major axis aligned with the primordium axis.
source: This confirmed that the SMC has a consistent anisotropic shape from early stages onwards, with a distinguishable major axis aligned with the primordium axis.
evidence: This is based on anisotropy analysis showing a mean angle of 22° (±11°, n = 16) between SMC major axis and ovule growth axis.

claim: The Reference Model combines an initial, narrow domain of anisotropic, signal-based growth with a high concentration in inner layers, a broad domain competent for passive strain-based relaxation, and material anisotropy.
source: This model combines the following hypotheses: an initial, narrow domain of anisotropic, signal-based growth with a high concentration in inner layers, a broad domain competent for passive strain-based relaxation, and material anisotropy (for FEM models only).
evidence: This describes the parameters of the reference computational model.

claim: Removing the growth anisotropy component abolished the digit shape of the primordium and produced a hemi-spherical protrusion in both FEM- and MS-based models.
source: Removing the growth anisotropy component abolished the digit shape of the primordium and produced a hemi-spherical protrusion in both FEM- and MS-based models (Figure 3B–F, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This demonstrates the necessity of growth anisotropy through model simulations shown in Figure 3.

claim: An inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth model, where the L1 also contributes to the expansion of the primordium, best described ovule primordium growth.
source: Notably, an inner tissue-driven growth model, where the L1 also contributes to the expansion of the primordium, best described ovule primordium growth.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of different model scenarios.

claim: Best-fit models produced by both cell- and tissue-based simulations predicted a growth-promoting signal in a confined domain along a vertical stripe at primordium emergence.
source: In addition, best-fit models produced by both cell- and tissue-based simulations predicted a growth-promoting signal in a confined domain along a vertical stripe at primordium emergence.
evidence: This prediction emerges from the modeling results.

claim: In the Reference Model (MS-Model 2), an L2 apical cell with a trapezoidal shape, elongated along the main direction of ovule growth, emerged consistently during simulation.
source: In the Reference Model (MS-Model 2), an L2 apical cell with a trapezoidal shape, elongated along the main direction of ovule growth, emerged consistently during simulation (note that these cells still divide in the models as no special rule has been assigned to them) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This emergent property is demonstrated in the simulation results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The elongated-trapezoidal shape of the SMC candidate emerges from the combination of assigned anisotropic cell growth and geometrical constraints imposed by the surrounding, growing tissues.
source: The elongated-trapezoidal shape of such a cell is not a prescribed feature of the model, but rather emerges from the combination of assigned anisotropic cell growth and geometrical constraints imposed by the surrounding, growing tissues.
evidence: This interpretation is based on analysis of the model behavior.

claim: Katanin mutant primordia are 1.5 times bigger in volume than wild-type primordia (p=0.007, stage 0-III).
source: kat mutant primordia clearly showed an increased size and a more isotropic shape (Figure 4A), being 1.5 times bigger in volume than wild-type primordia (p=0.007, stage 0-III, Figure 4B) with a smaller aspect ratio (p<0.01 stages 1-I, 1-II, Figure 4C).
evidence: This quantitative difference is demonstrated with statistical significance in Figure 4B.

claim: Katanin mutant primordia have a smaller aspect ratio than wild-type (p<0.01 stages 1-I, 1-II).
source: kat mutant primordia clearly showed an increased size and a more isotropic shape (Figure 4A), being 1.5 times bigger in volume than wild-type primordia (p=0.007, stage 0-III, Figure 4B) with a smaller aspect ratio (p<0.01 stages 1-I, 1-II, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At stage 0-III, kat ovules display a broader epidermis domain composed of more and larger cells than wild-type ovules (p=0.03 and p<0.001, respectively).
source: Indeed, at stage 0-III, kat ovules display a broader epidermis domain composed of more and larger cells than wild-type ovules (p=0.03 and p<0.001, respectively) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This finding is based on domain-specific cell quantification shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mitosis frequency analysis in kat mutants indicated a shift in cell division from the apex toward the basis (2.4 times less mitoses in the L1 dome domain and 2.7 times more in the L1 basal domain, compared to the wild type).
source: Mitosis frequency analysis indicated a shift in cell division from the apex toward the basis (2.4 times less mitoses in the L1 dome domain and 2.7 times more in the L1 basal domain, compared to the wild type) (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E), consistent with the increased cell number observed in L1.
evidence: This is based on CYCB1.1db-GFP reporter analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: At stage 1-II, 34% of the kat primordia (n = 109) showed more than one enlarged, subepidermal cell; decreasing to 14% at stage 2-II (n = 104).
source: At stage 1-II, 34% of the kat primordia (n = 109) showed more than one enlarged, subepidermal cell; decreasing to 14% at stage 2-II (n = 104), in stark contrast with wild-type primordia showing a majority (86% to 96%) of primordia with an unambiguous, single SMC (Figure 5C).
evidence: This quantification is based on analysis of cleared ovule primordia shown in Figure 5C.

claim: H1.1-GFP eviction occurred in more than one cell in 29% of kat primordia (n = 43).
source: H1.1-GFP eviction occurred in more than one cell in 29% of kat primordia (n = 43, Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the H1.1-GFP marker shown in Figure 5D.

claim: KNU-YFP was ectopically expressed in 21% of kat primordia at stage 1-II (n = 43).
source: Detectable as early as stage 1-I in the wild type, it was ectopically expressed in 21% of kat primordia at stage 1-II (n = 43) (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the KNU-YFP marker shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ectopic expression of AtDMC1-GUS was scored in 57% of kat primordia (n = 56).
source: Third, to test whether the ectopic SMC candidates have a meiotic competence, we analyzed the AtDMC1-GUS reporter (Agashe et al., 2002; Klimyuk and Jones, 1997) and, indeed, scored ectopic expression in 57% of kat primordia (n = 56) (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is based on GUS staining analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Using aniline blue staining, ectopic cells accumulating callose or ectopic tetrads were never detected in kat ovules (n = 119 and 269 ovules in bot1-7 and lue1, respectively).
source: However, using aniline blue staining of callose deposition, which in wild-type SMCs stains the cell wall immediately before meiosis and marks the cells walls of tetrads after meiosis, we never detected ectopic cells accumulating callose or ectopic tetrads in kat ovules (n = 119 and 269 ovules in bot1-7 and lue1, respectively) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This negative result is based on callose staining analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: 21% kat primordia (n = 29) showed two cells labeled with pWOX2-CenH3-GFP marker at FG1 stage, as compared to 4% (n = 26) in the wild type.
source: We next analyzed the pWOX2-CenH3-GFP marker labeling centromeres starting at the functional megaspore stage (FG1 stage) (De Storme et al., 2016) and found 21% kat primordia (n = 29) with two labeled cells, as compared to 4% (n = 26) in the wild type (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the centromere marker shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: In the wild type, 27% of primordia (n = 289) had two SMC candidates (Class B) at stage 0-II, this frequency decreasing to 3% at stage 2-II (n = 103).
source: In the wild type, the majority of ovules showed a single candidate SMC (Class A) at stage 0-II but 27% of primordia (n = 289) had two SMC candidates (Class B), this frequency decreasing to 3% at stage 2-II (n = 103).
evidence: This quantification demonstrates the progressive restriction of SMC fate.

claim: In wild-type primordia, SMC singleness is largely resolved at stage 1-I.
source: Thus, instead of being immediate, SMC singleness can arise from a progressive restriction of fate among several SMC candidates during development. In wild-type primordia, SMC singleness is largely resolved at stage 1-I (Figure 6B).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the developmental time course shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Plasticity in SMC emergence is higher in kat mutants with 42% (n = 202) class B primordia at stage 0-II compared to 26% (n = 289) in the wild type.
source: Clearly, plasticity is higher with 42% (n = 202) class B primordia at stage 0-II in kat compared to 26% (n = 289) in the wild type.
evidence: This comparison demonstrates increased plasticity in kat mutants.

claim: The resolution process is delayed in kat mutants as up to 33% Class B primordia persist at stage 1-II (n = 113) compared to 12% in the wild type (n = 281).
source: In addition, the resolution process is delayed in kat mutants as up to 33% Class B primordia persist at stage 1-II (n = 113) compared to 12% in the wild type (n = 281).
evidence: This demonstrates delayed canalization in kat mutants.

claim: Wild-type Class A and B primordia showed an enlarged nucleus in the candidate SMCs from stage 0-II onwards.
source: Wild-type Class A and B primordia showed an enlarged nucleus in the candidate SMCs from stage 0-II onwards, and this correlation was also true in kat primordia (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is based on nuclear area measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In Phase I wild-type primordia, an S-phase pattern was captured in ~24% (n = 112) and ~40% (n = 79) of Class A primordia at stage 0-II and 0-III, respectively.
source: This pattern was captured in a large proportion of primordia at stage 0-II and 0-III: ~24% (n = 112) and ~40% (n = 79) for Class A, respectively; 30% (n = 41) and 28% (n = 60) for Class B, respectively (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is based on PCNA-GFP reporter analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: In Phase II, SMC candidates showed no S-phase pattern in a large majority of both Class A and B primordia (97% on average, over entire Phase II).
source: In Phase II, SMC candidates showed no S-phase pattern in a large majority of both Class A and B primordia (97% on average, over entire Phase II) (Figure 6G–H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1G–H) in agreement with the presence of newly replicated DNA at stage 1-I (She et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on PCNA-GFP analysis shown in Figure 6G-H and supported by cited literature.

claim: In Phase II, kat primordia display a higher frequency of S-phase patterns in SMC candidates, suggesting that S-phase duration or entry is delayed compared to the wild type.
source: Strikingly, in Phase II, kat primordia display a higher frequency of S-phase patterns in SMC candidates (Figure 6H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,H), suggesting that S-phase duration or entry is delayed compared to the wild type.
evidence: This finding is based on PCNA-GFP analysis and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: The ovule primordium emerges from the placenta as a small dome-shaped protrusion and grows into a digit-shaped primordium with nearly cylindrical symmetry (stage 1-I) before enlarging at the base.
source: The ovule primordium emerges from the placenta as a small dome-shaped protrusion and grows into a digit-shaped primordium with nearly cylindrical symmetry (stage 1-I) before enlarging at the base (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the morphological progression observed in the study.

claim: The temporal resolution of the analysis led to subdivision of early stages (stage 0-I to stage 0-III) covering primordium emergence prior to the straight digit-shape of the organ set as stage 1-I.
source: The temporal resolution of our analysis led us to subdivide early stages (stage 0-I to stage 0-III) covering primordium emergence prior to the straight digit-shape of the organ set as stage 1-I, where the SMC becomes distinguishable by its apparent larger size in longitudinal views (Grossniklaus and Schneitz, 1998; Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the refined staging system developed in this study.

claim: Companion cells showed an increasing ellipticity (and decreasing sphericity), starting at stage 1-I and culminating at stage 2-I.
source: Companion cells showed an increasing ellipticity (and decreasing sphericity), starting at stage 1-I and culminating at stage 2-I (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on shape analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The averaged maximum anisotropy shape index of the SMCs was consistently above the medium (and hence above the minimum) anisotropy index.
source: The averaged maximum anisotropy shape index of the SMCs was consistently above the medium (and hence above the minimum) anisotropy index (Figure 2K, Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is based on anisotropy analysis shown in Figure 2K.

claim: The mean angle between SMC major axis and ovule growth axis at stage 0-II was 22° (±11°, n = 16).
source: We measured the degree of alignment of the SMC major axis with the main growth axis of the ovule during early stages (stage 0-II) and found a mean angle of 22° (±11°, n = 16) (Figure 2K).
evidence: This quantitative measurement is shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Two complementary 2D models of ovule primordium growth were developed: a finite element method (FEM)-based mechanical model and a mass spring (MS)-based model.
source: For this, we developed two complementary 2D models of a longitudinal section of the ovule intersecting its main elongation axis: (i) a finite element method FEM-based mechanical model of the ovule represented as a continuous object (only outlining L1 vs. inner L2,L3 tissue) and (ii) a mass spring MS-based model of the ovule able to represent the mechanical status of each cell wall.
evidence: This describes the modeling approaches used in the study.

claim: Growth was implemented using two uncoupled but complementary modalities: signal-based growth and strain-based growth.
source: Growth was implemented in both frameworks using two uncoupled but complementary modalities: (i) growth in which an abstract growth factor captures the cumulative effects of biochemical signals without considering their explicit mode of action (i.e. cell wall loosening, increasing turgor pressure), hereafter referred to as 'signal-based growth' (Boudon et al., 2015; Coen et al., 2004); and (ii) passive growth through relaxation of excess of strain inside the tissue, hereafter referred as 'strain-based growth' (Boudon et al., 2015; Bozorg et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the modeling framework with citations to prior work.

claim: When the growth signal is absent in the inner L2,L3 tissue, signal growth in the L1 alone is not sufficient to enable primordium growth.
source: When the growth signal is absent in the inner L2,L3 tissue (FEM-Model 6, MS-Model 6), signal growth in the L1 alone is not sufficient to enable primordium growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This conclusion is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both models where a high level of growth signal is selectively present in L1 or in inner L2,L3 layers can produce a digit-shaped primordium.
source: To conclude, both models where a high level of growth signal is selectively present in L1 or in inner L2,L3 layers can produce a digit-shaped primordium.
evidence: This conclusion is based on comparison of different model scenarios.

claim: Absence of a growth signal in the inner L2,L3 layers results in drastic shape alterations, favoring a scenario where inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth plays a fundamental role.
source: Yet, absence of a growth signal in the inner L2,L3 layers results in drastic shape alterations. This favors a scenario where inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth plays a fundamental role.
evidence: This interpretation is based on model results.

claim: A broad tissue domain uniformly competent for strain accommodation is necessary to resolve the high accumulation of stress, which limits primordium elongation.
source: Next, through modulation of passive strain-based growth, we determined that a broad tissue domain uniformly competent for strain accommodation is necessary to resolve the high accumulation of stress, which limits primordium elongation (FEM-Model 8, MS-Model 8, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This conclusion is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Even in the case of isotropic material, it is possible to grow a digit-shaped protrusion, yet with a wider dome and increased L1 thickness, contrasting experimental observations.
source: We also explored the contribution of material anisotropy for FEM-based simulations (FEM-Model 2 and FEM-Model 2a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C): even in the case of isotropic material, it is possible to grow a digit-shaped protrusion, yet with a wider dome and increased L1 thickness, contrasting experimental observations.
evidence: This finding is based on FEM model simulations.

claim: To restore L1 thickness in models with isotropic material, it is sufficient to prescribe material anisotropy exclusively in the L1.
source: To restore L1 thickness, it is sufficient to prescribe material anisotropy exclusively in the L1 (FEM-Model 2a).
evidence: This is based on FEM model simulations.

claim: The SMC candidate does not display the stereotypical elongated, trapezoidal shape in MS-Model 3 with isotropic cell growth in inner layers.
source: As Figure 3G–H shows, the SMC candidate does not display the stereotypical shape and is not even elongated.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the model simulations shown in Figure 3G-H.

claim: Mild cell anisotropy can be reached in the SMC candidate if it is allowed to grow twice more than in the Reference Model.
source: Yet, mild cell anisotropy can be reached if the SMC candidate is allowed to grow twice more than in the Reference Model (MS-Model 3a, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is shown in model simulations in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Directional cell growth in the epidermis is necessary to accommodate inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth and permit primordium elongation.
source: The complementary model, altering cell growth anisotropy specifically in the L1, further suggested that directional cell growth in the epidermis is necessary to accommodate inner L2,L3 layer-driven growth and permit primordium elongation (MS-Model 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This conclusion is based on model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: When the SMC candidate was prevented from dividing in simulations, its enlargement overrode primordium shape control, creating an enlarged dome.
source: When we prevented the SMC candidate to divide, its enlargement overrode primordium shape control in our simulations, creating an enlarged dome (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is demonstrated in model simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: A mechanism may limit SMC growth in real ovule primordia to prevent overriding primordium shape control.
source: This suggests that a mechanism may limit SMC growth in real ovule primordia.
evidence: This is inferred from the model behavior when SMC division is prevented.

claim: In absence of the microtubule-severing protein KATANIN, the self-organization of cortical microtubules in parallel arrays is hindered, thereby decreasing the cellulose-dependent mechanical anisotropy of the cell wall, resulting in more isotropic growth.
source: in absence of the microtubule-severing protein KATANIN, the self-organization of cortical microtubules in parallel arrays is hindered, thereby decreasing the cellulose-dependent mechanical anisotropy of the cell wall, resulting in more isotropic growth (Bichet et al., 2001; Burk and Ye, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about KATANIN function supported by cited literature.

claim: KATANIN is expressed ubiquitously in the ovule, including both epidermal and internal L2,L3 tissue layers.
source: Note that KAT is expressed ubiquitously and, thus, also in the ovule: the KATANIN protein could be detected in both epidermal and internal L2,L3 tissue layers using a GFP reporter (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated using a GFP reporter shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutant primordia are clearly distinct from wild-type primordia in their relationship between aspect ratio and bounding box occupancy at stage 1-I.
source: Mutant primordia are clearly distinct from wild-type primordia in their relationship between aspect ratio and bounding box occupancy at stage 1-I (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), when the primordium normally starts elongating along the major growth axis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: These measurements confirmed a marked attenuation of anisotropic growth in kat ovule primordia as was observed in roots, shoot organs, or seeds.
source: These measurements confirmed a marked attenuation of anisotropic growth in kat ovule primordia as was observed in roots, shoot organs, or seeds (Bichet et al., 2001; Hervieux et al., 2016; Luptovčiak et al., 2017b; Ren et al., 2017; Uyttewaal et al., 2012; Wightman et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This finding is consistent with prior observations in other tissues supported by cited literature.

claim: At a global level, the mean cell number, cell volume, and sphericity are not significantly different between kat and wild-type primordia.
source: Yet, at a global level, the mean cell number, cell volume, and sphericity are not significantly different between kat and wild-type primordia (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–C).
evidence: This is based on global quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: In kat SMC neighbors at stage 0-II, there is an increased relative frequency of CYCB1.1db-GFP expression, whereas it decreases at stage 1-II.
source: When specifically looking at the L2 apical domain, where the SMC differentiates, we noticed an increased relative frequency of CYCB1.1db-GFP expression in kat SMC neighbors at stage 0-II, whereas it decreases at stage 1-II (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on mitotic reporter analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: This is in stark contrast with SMC neighbors in wild-type primordia displaying first a relative mitotic quiescence at stage 0-II, and then enhanced mitotic activity at stage 1-II.
source: This is in stark contrast with SMC neighbors in wild-type primordia displaying first a relative mitotic quiescence at stage 0-II, and then enhanced mitotic activity at stage 1-II.
evidence: This comparison highlights the altered temporal pattern in kat mutants.

claim: In the SMC, no mitotic activity increase was observed in kat as compared to wild-type primordia.
source: Yet, in the SMC, no mitotic activity increase was observed in kat as compared to wild-type primordia (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is based on mitotic reporter analysis.

claim: The most parsimonious hypothesis is that the altered geometry in kat primordia expands the domain of cells competent to form SMCs.
source: The most parsimonious hypothesis is that the altered geometry in kat primordia expands the domain of cells competent to form SMCs.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the kat phenotype.

claim: Isotropic cell growth and altered mechanical constraints in the tissue acting from primordia emergence onwards lead to divisions and patterning alterations that expand the domain of cells competent for SMC fate.
source: In this scenario, isotropic cell growth and altered mechanical constraints in the tissue acting from primordia emergence onwards, lead to divisions and patterning alterations that expand the domain of cells competent for SMC fate.
evidence: This is the proposed working model based on the data.

claim: SMC candidates emerge from within a mitotically quiescent L2 apical domain.
source: We found that SMC candidates emerge from within a mitotically quiescent L2 apical domain, consistent with the finding that the H3.1 histone variant HTR13 is evicted, marking cell cycle exit (Hernandez-Lagana and Autran, 2020).
evidence: This finding is consistent with cited work on histone variant eviction.

claim: SMC candidates have a markedly long S-phase compared to surrounding cells.
source: In addition, SMC candidates have a markedly long S-phase compared to surrounding cells.
evidence: This is based on PCNA-GFP reporter analysis.

claim: These observations are reminiscent of the animal germline where mitotic quiescence is a prerequisite for meiosis.
source: These observations are reminiscent of the animal germline where mitotic quiescence is a prerequisite for meiosis (Kimble, 2011; Reik and Surani, 2015).
evidence: This comparison to animal systems is supported by cited literature.

claim: Early SMC candidates already display a typically large cell and nucleus size and an elongated shape aligned with the primordium growth axis.
source: Also, early SMC candidates already display a typically large cell and nucleus size and an elongated shape aligned with the primordium growth axis.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of cell and nuclear characteristics.

claim: SMC characteristics are established much earlier than previously thought, that is, soon after primordium emergence (stages 0-II/0-III).
source: Collectively, we found that SMC characteristics are established much earlier than previously thought, that is, soon after primordium emergence (stages 0-II/0 III).
evidence: This is a key finding that revises previous understanding.

claim: These characteristics frequently arise in more than one SMC candidate at Phase I, typically resolving into a single SMC at the onset of Phase II.
source: Moreover, these characteristics frequently arise in more than one SMC candidate at Phase I, typically resolving into a single SMC at the onset of Phase II.
evidence: This describes the temporal dynamics of SMC fate restriction.

claim: This clearly documents a developmental sequence of plasticity at SMC fate emergence and progressive resolution of SMC fate to a single cell.
source: This clearly documents a developmental sequence of plasticity at SMC fate emergence and progressive resolution of SMC fate to a single cell.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of the developmental progression.

claim: This is reminiscent of developmental canalization, which refers to the capacity of an organism to follow a given developmental trajectory in spite of disturbances.
source: This is reminiscent of developmental canalization, which refers to the capacity of an organism to follow a given developmental trajectory in spite of disturbances (Hallgrimsson et al., 2019; Scharloo, 1991; Waddington, 1942).
evidence: This conceptual framework is supported by cited literature on canalization.

claim: Cell fate canalization is well studied in animal systems where it is modulated by intercellular signal-based feedback mechanisms, epigenetic regulation, and organ geometry.
source: Cell fate canalization is well studied in animal systems where it is modulated by intercellular signal-based feedback mechanisms (Heitzler and Simpson, 1991), epigenetic regulation (Pujadas and Feinberg, 2012), and organ geometry (Huang et al., 2020; Huang and Russell, 1992; Pujadas and Feinberg, 2012; Royer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge from animal developmental biology supported by citations.

claim: In plants, canalization is better known in the context of organogenesis during phyllotaxis and developmental robustness.
source: In plants, canalization is better known in the context of organogenesis during phyllotaxis and developmental robustness (Godin et al., 2020; Lempe et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from plant developmental biology supported by citations.

claim: This study expands the examples of canalization to the level of a cellular domain in the Arabidopsis ovule primordium.
source: Our study expands the examples of canalization to the level of a cellular domain in the Arabidopsis ovule primordium.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and contribution of the study.

claim: While L2 apical cells initially share the competence to form SMC candidates, leading to plasticity at SMC emergence, the progressive restriction of cell fate possibilities in the primordium apex ultimately leads to the specification of only one SMC committed to meiosis.
source: While L2 apical cells initially share the competence to form SMC candidates, leading to plasticity at SMC emergence, the progressive restriction of cell fate possibilities in the primordium apex ultimately leads to the specification of only one SMC committed to meiosis.
evidence: This summarizes the canalization process observed in the study.

claim: The results are in line with a formerly proposed canalization process operating during SMC establishment.
source: Our results are in line with a formerly proposed canalization process operating during SMC establishment (Grossniklaus and Schneitz, 1998; Rodríguez-Leal et al., 2015).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior hypotheses in the literature.

claim: Despite several mutations altering SMC singleness in Arabidopsis, including kat, canalization remains a robust process securing the formation of a single embryo sac despite such genetic perturbations.
source: Despite the fact that several mutations (reviewed in Pinto et al., 2019; Mendes et al., 2020), including kat (this study), alter SMC singleness in Arabidopsis, canalization remains a robust process securing the formation of a single embryo sac despite such genetic perturbations.
evidence: This highlights the robustness of the canalization process.

claim: SMC fate emergence is characterized by mitotic quiescence and cellular growth in one or more L2 apical cells.
source: SMC fate emergence is characterized by mitotic quiescence and cellular growth in one or more L2 apical cells.
evidence: This summarizes key cellular events associated with SMC emergence.

claim: SMC singleness resolution is associated with re-entry into a somatic cell cycle and re-incorporation of a replicative histone H3.1 in candidates neighboring the SMC.
source: SMC singleness resolution is associated with re-entry into a somatic cell cycle (this study), and re-incorporation of a replicative histone H3.1 (Hernandez-Lagana and Autran, 2020) in candidates neighboring the SMC.
evidence: This describes cellular events during fate resolution, with one aspect cited from prior work.

claim: Similar to mouse and Drosophila, where tissue mechanics and organ geometry were shown to contribute to cell fate canalization, ovule primordium geometry contributes to channel SMC fate in the apex and the resolution into a single SMC.
source: Similar to mouse and Drosophila, where tissue mechanics and organ geometry were shown to contribute to cell fate canalization (Chan et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2020; Royer et al., 2020), we propose that ovule primordium geometry contributes to channel SMC fate in the apex and the resolution into a single SMC.
evidence: This draws a parallel to animal systems and proposes a mechanism based on the study's findings.

claim: In kat, increased plasticity and delayed resolution process toward SMC singleness occurs.
source: In this conceptual framework, kat increases plasticity and delays the resolution process toward SMC singleness (working model Figure 6I).
evidence: This is part of the working model presented in Figure 6I.

claim: The work proposes a conceptual framework linking organ geometry, cell shape, and cell fate acquisition in the ovule primordium, which is potentially of broader relevance in plant patterning.
source: Altogether, our work proposes a conceptual framework linking organ geometry, cell shape, and cell fate acquisition in the ovule primordium, which is potentially of broader relevance in plant patterning.
evidence: This is a claim about the broader significance of the work.

claim: The image resource published in this study is complementary to others capturing ovule development at later stages.
source: In addition, the image resource published in this study is complementary to others capturing ovule development at later stages (Lora et al., 2017; Vijayan et al., 2021).
evidence: This positions the resource in the context of existing datasets.

claim: The dataset populates a growing number of 3D-segmented images of plant tissues and organs, which collectively build the fundament of a developmental atlas integrating morphogenesis with gene expression.
source: It also populates a growing number of 3D-segmented images of plant tissues and organs (Wolny et al., 2020), which collectively build the fundament of a developmental atlas integrating morphogenesis with gene expression (Hartmann et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the broader context and potential impact of the resource.
